manure-storage-volume.formula: manure_volume = (daily_manure + wastewater + bedding) x storage_days; precip_storm_volume = surface_area x (net_precip + storm) / 12; freeboard_volume = surface_area x freeboard_in / 12; total = the sum.
manure-storage-volume.edition: NRCS Conservation Practice Standard 313 / ASABE D384 manure production, by name.
manure-storage-volume.freeAccess: NRCS 313 and ASABE D384 are public standards; the engineer/planner of record governs the actual design.
manure-storage-volume.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
manure-storage-volume.editionNote: An uncovered liquid facility must bank the net precipitation and the 25-year, 24-hour storm falling on its own surface over the storage period - sizing to manure alone overtops in a wet spring. CPS 313 sets no fixed minimum storage period; under 120 days is flagged as short, a common nutrient-management-plan floor, and freeboard is 6 inches for a vertical-wall tank and 12 inches for other structures. NRCS 313 and the engineer/planner govern - a planning aid, not the engineer of record.

chimney-height-for-draft.formula: T_o_R = ambient_temp_f + 460; T_m_R = mean_flue_temp_f + 460; H = target_draft_net_inwc / (net_factor x 0.52 x baro_psia x (1/T_o_R - 1/T_m_R)) [ft]; the inverse of D_net = net_factor x 0.52 x B x H x (1/T_o - 1/T_m).
chimney-height-for-draft.edition: ASHRAE Handbook HVAC Systems (chimney/vent) / NFPA 211 theoretical chimney draft solved for the stack height, by name.
chimney-height-for-draft.freeAccess: The theoretical-draft relation is standard chimney/vent design practice; the venting standard and appliance instructions govern the actual sign-off.
chimney-height-for-draft.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
chimney-height-for-draft.editionNote: The stack height needed to produce a target NET draft, the inverse of the chimney-draft tile: H = D_net_target / (net_factor x 0.52 x B x (1/T_o - 1/T_m)) with temperatures absolute (Rankine). Enter the net draft the appliance actually needs; the net_factor of 0.5 to 0.8 already accounts for flow and fitting losses off the theoretical no-flow draft. The barometric pressure must be altitude-corrected because thinner air at elevation cuts the draft, so a taller stack is needed higher up, and T_m is the mean flue temperature, not the outlet. The venting standard (NFPA 211) and the appliance instructions govern - a design aid, not a venting sign-off.

assumptions.name: Net-draft target
assumptions.value: the target is the net available draft; the net_factor (0.5 to 0.8) already removes flow and fitting losses from the theoretical no-flow draft

assumptions.name: Altitude and absolute temps
assumptions.value: barometric pressure must be altitude-corrected; temperatures are absolute (Rankine), T_m the mean flue temp

cattle-stocking-rate.editionNote: One animal unit (AU) = a 1,000 lb cow consuming ~26 lb dry matter/day; one AUM = 790 lb (26 lb x 30.4 days). Drought and climate adjustments are essential and not modeled. Forage production from a clip-and-weigh sample or the NRCS Ecological Site Description governs.

assumptions.source: NRCS National Range and Pasture Handbook

assumptions.name: Animal-unit equivalents

motor-pole-identification.formula: pole-pairs = floor(60 x f / rpm) (a speed up to 5% above a synchronous speed keeps that pole count and is flagged); poles = 2 x pole-pairs; Ns = 120 x f / poles; slip = (Ns - rpm) / Ns.
motor-pole-identification.edition: First-principles AC-machine speed relation Ns = 120 x f / P inverted to identify the poles; classical induction-machine theory.
motor-pole-identification.freeAccess: First-principles physics; no licensed source required.
motor-pole-identification.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
motor-pole-identification.editionNote: The inverse of the synchronous-speed relation: given the nameplate full-load speed and the line frequency, identify the pole count. Because the synchronous speed sits just above the running speed, the pole count is the even number at or below 120 x f / rpm - pole-pairs = floor(60 x f / rpm), poles = 2 x pole-pairs (an 800 rpm Design D motor is 8-pole, not 10) - and then the synchronous speed Ns = 120 x f / poles and slip = (Ns - rpm)/Ns follow. If the entered speed is at or above the identified synchronous speed the slip is zero or negative, which an induction-motor nameplate never shows, so the rpm or frequency should be rechecked. The nameplate and the manufacturer govern.

assumptions.name: Poles at or below the ratio
assumptions.value: poles = 2 x floor(60 x f / rpm); the synchronous speed sits just above the running speed

assumptions.name: Induction machine
assumptions.value: the nameplate speed is below synchronous; a zero/negative slip flags a bad rpm or frequency

helical-pile.freeAccess: ICC-ES AC358 free at icc-es.org. Manufacturer Kt values free in each manufacturer's published evaluation report.
helical-pile.governance: Estimate. Engineer of record governs the design and acceptance. Verify against the project structural drawings and the manufacturer's published capacity / chart.
helical-pile.editionNote: Single-edition (manufacturer Kt benchmarks; quarterly recheck per spec-v7 §8). The engineer of record specifies the project Kt and acceptance torque.

assumptions.name: Kt table

assumptions.name: Default factor of safety
assumptions.value: 2.0 unless user supplies (engineering-practice default for axial helical piers)

solar-thermal-collector.formula: efficiency = optical_efficiency - loss_coeff x (inlet_temp_f - ambient_temp_f) / irradiance_btu; useful_btu_per_sqft = irradiance_btu x max(0, efficiency); useful_btu_hr = useful_btu_per_sqft x area_sqft.
solar-thermal-collector.edition: Flat-plate solar thermal collector efficiency (ASHRAE 93 / Hottel-Whillier-Bliss line as reported by the SRCC collector rating), by name; the SRCC-rated intercept and slope, the incidence angle, the flow rate, and the glazing condition govern the real output.
solar-thermal-collector.freeAccess: The collector efficiency line is public solar-engineering theory (ASHRAE 93 / Hottel-Whillier-Bliss); the intercept and slope come from the collector's SRCC rating and the temperatures and sun from the site.
solar-thermal-collector.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
solar-thermal-collector.editionNote: A flat-plate solar thermal collector's instantaneous efficiency falls on a straight line, the model behind every SRCC collector rating and the ASHRAE 93 test: efficiency equals the optical efficiency (the y-intercept, the product of the heat-removal factor FR and the transmittance-absorptance tau-alpha, about 0.68 to 0.75 for a good glazed flat plate) minus a loss term that grows as the collector runs hotter than the surrounding air. That loss term is the loss coefficient (FR times the overall loss coefficient UL, the slope of the line) multiplied by the difference between the fluid inlet temperature and the ambient air temperature, divided by the solar irradiance striking the collector. The optical efficiency is the best the collector can do, reached only when the fluid enters at ambient temperature; every degree the fluid runs above ambient, and every drop in sunshine, pulls the efficiency down. With an optical efficiency of 0.70, a loss coefficient of 0.85 Btu per hour per square foot per degree F, a 120 F inlet, 70 F ambient, and 300 Btu per hour per square foot of sun, the efficiency is 0.70 minus 0.85 times 50 divided by 300, or 0.56, so the collector delivers 300 times 0.56 = 168 Btu per hour per square foot, and 6,700 Btu per hour over a 40 square foot panel. On a colder, dimmer day -- a 140 F inlet, 40 F ambient, and only 250 Btu per hour per square foot -- the efficiency drops to 0.36 and the output to 3,600 Btu per hour, illustrating that a collector is least efficient exactly when heating demand is highest. Beyond the stagnation point, where the efficiency reaches zero, the collector gives no useful heat at all. An unglazed pool collector has a near-unity optical efficiency but a very steep loss slope, which is why it is useful only when operated close to ambient temperature. This is a performance estimate; the collector's actual SRCC-rated intercept and slope, the solar incidence angle, the fluid flow rate, and the glazing condition govern the real output.

assumptions.name: ASHRAE 93 efficiency line
assumptions.value: eta = FR(ta) - FR*UL*(Ti - Ta)/G; useful heat = G x max(0, eta) x area; intercept ~0.68-0.75 glazed flat plate

assumptions.name: Operating point
assumptions.value: least efficient when hot and dim; no useful heat past stagnation (eta <= 0); unglazed pool collectors have a high intercept but steep loss slope

joist-notch-bore-limit.formula: end_notch_max = D/4; notch_depth_max = D/6; notch_length_max = D/3; bore_dia_max = D/3; bore_edge_min = 2 in (D = actual joist depth).
joist-notch-bore-limit.edition: IRC R502.8.1 sawn-lumber floor-joist notching and boring limits, by name; the fractions apply to the actual joist depth. The AHJ-adopted IRC edition governs.
joist-notch-bore-limit.freeAccess: The fractional limits are prescriptive IRC R502.8.1 values (many jurisdictions post the adopted IRC); the tile applies them to the entered actual joist depth.
joist-notch-bore-limit.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
joist-notch-bore-limit.editionNote: IRC R502.8.1 limits on notching and boring SAWN-LUMBER floor joists, applied to the ACTUAL joist depth (a 2x10 is 9.25 in, a 2x12 is 11.25 in). A notch at the bearing ends may not exceed one quarter of the depth (D/4). A notch elsewhere on the top or bottom edge is limited to D/6 in depth and D/3 in length, and notches are NOT permitted in the middle third of the span. A bored hole may not exceed D/3 in diameter, and its edge must be at least 2 in from the top and bottom edges of the joist and at least 2 in from any other hole or notch. These prescriptive limits are for dimension lumber ONLY -- engineered I-joists, LVL, and trusses follow the manufacturer's hole chart and web-stiffener rules, and a flange must never be field-notched. A cantilever, a doubled/built-up member, or a heavily loaded joist may be more restrictive, and the AHJ-adopted code and any engineering govern.

assumptions.name: Actual depth
assumptions.value: fractions apply to the actual dressed depth (2x10 = 9.25 in, 2x12 = 11.25 in), not the nominal

assumptions.name: Sawn lumber only
assumptions.value: engineered I-joists / LVL / trusses follow the maker's hole chart; never notch a flange

flat-top-stockpile-volume.formula: Rb = base_diameter/2, Rt = top_diameter/2; height = (Rb - Rt) x tan(repose x pi/180); volume = (pi height/3)(Rb^2 + Rb Rt + Rt^2); volume_cy = volume/27; tons = volume x density/2000.
flat-top-stockpile-volume.edition: Truncated-cone (frustum) stockpile geometry by name (angle-of-repose flat-topped pile); first-principles geometry.
flat-top-stockpile-volume.freeAccess: The frustum-volume and angle-of-repose relations are public geometry and soil-mechanics practice.
flat-top-stockpile-volume.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
flat-top-stockpile-volume.editionNote: A flat-topped stockpile - the truncated cone (frustum) a radial stacker or a bulldozer leaves when it cannot peak the pile - from the base diameter, the flat-top diameter, and the angle of repose: the side slope sets the height h = (base_radius - top_radius) tan(repose), and the volume is the frustum (pi h/3)(Rb^2 + Rb Rt + Rt^2). Set the top diameter to 0 and it collapses to the sharp conical stockpile-volume pile. The angle of repose depends on the material and its moisture (roughly 30-40 degrees for granular material) and steepens as the material gets damp or angular; an irregular base or a non-level top change it. A survey volume governs for payment.

assumptions.name: Shape
assumptions.value: truncated cone (frustum); height from the repose slope; top diameter 0 gives the sharp cone

assumptions.name: Angle of repose
assumptions.value: 37 degrees default (granular material runs ~30-40 degrees); moisture and angularity steepen it

assumptions.name: Bulk density
assumptions.value: 100 pcf default loose (the material governs); a survey governs for payment

detention-basin-volume.formula: Required volume = target detention time × flow (the inverse of detention time = volume / flow). Sizes chlorine-contact (CT), flocculation, and sedimentation basins to a target contact/detention time.
detention-basin-volume.edition: Recommended Standards for Water Works (Ten States Standards), latest edition, by name. EPA Surface Water Treatment Rule (SWTR) 40 CFR 141 Subpart H by section for CT.
detention-basin-volume.freeAccess: 40 CFR 141 free at ecfr.gov. Ten States Standards published by the Great Lakes - Upper Mississippi River Board.
detention-basin-volume.governance: Estimate. Operator of record and primacy agency govern.
detention-basin-volume.editionNote: The theoretical (plug-flow) basin volume from a target detention time. The state primacy agency governs.

rainwater-catchment-area.formula: catchment_ft2 = target_annual_gal / (annual_in x 0.6233 x efficiency); the inverse of annual_gal = area x rainfall x 0.6233 x efficiency.
rainwater-catchment-area.edition: ARCSA (American Rainwater Catchment Systems Association) Rainwater Harvesting Manual by name; NOAA precipitation data.
rainwater-catchment-area.freeAccess: ARCSA materials free at arcsa.org. NOAA precipitation data free at hdsc.nws.noaa.gov.
rainwater-catchment-area.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed plumber / gas fitter govern. Verify against the IPC / IFGC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
rainwater-catchment-area.editionNote: The catchment (roof) footprint needed to harvest a target annual volume, the inverse of rainwater-yield: area = target_gal / (annual_in x 0.6233 x efficiency). The 0.6233 converts one inch of rain over one square foot to gallons; efficiency (installers assume 0.75 to 0.90 per the TWDB Rainwater Harvesting Manual; 0.85 default) accounts for first-flush, splash, and evaporation losses. The area is the horizontal footprint the rain falls on, not the sloped surface. Single-edition (ARCSA + NOAA precipitation data). A planning estimate; local rainfall records, the storage tank size, and the demand pattern govern the real system.

assumptions.name: Conversion and efficiency
assumptions.value: 0.6233 gal per in-ft^2; collection efficiency 0.75 to 0.90 (TWDB), 0.85 default

assumptions.name: Horizontal footprint
assumptions.value: the area is the horizontal projected footprint, not the sloped roof surface

gobo-image-size.formula: image_diameter_ft = 2 x throw_ft x tan(phi), phi = field_angle_deg / 2; stretched_axis_ft = throw_ft x sin(phi) x [1/cos(incidence - phi) + 1/cos(incidence + phi)] (the two edge rays meeting the tilted surface); keystone_stretch = stretched_axis_ft / image_diameter_ft; relative_illuminance = cos(incidence_deg) at the beam centre; no finite image once incidence + phi reaches 90 degrees.
gobo-image-size.edition: Gobo image size from the field-angle cone, with the long axis from the edge rays meeting the tilted surface and the cos illuminance falloff for a non-perpendicular hit, by name; public projection geometry. The fixture's published field angle and a focus check in the room govern.
gobo-image-size.freeAccess: The projection geometry is public. The throw, field angle, incidence angle, and gobo dimensions are the designer's own values.
gobo-image-size.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
gobo-image-size.editionNote: A gobo fills the fixture's field, so the projected image is the field-angle cone intersected with the surface it lands on. Straight on that is a circle whose diameter is twice the throw times the tangent of half the field angle -- the same geometry as the beam pool, applied to the image rather than to the light. Off perpendicular the circle becomes an ellipse, and the asymmetry is the whole problem: the axis lying in the plane of the tilt stretches while the perpendicular axis stays near its straight-on width, which is what turns a projected logo into a trapezoid. The stretch is larger than the narrow-beam one-over-cosine rule because the far edge of the beam lands at a flatter angle than the centre: for a 36-degree field it is 1.58 at forty-five degrees and 2.93 at sixty, and once the incidence plus half the field reaches ninety degrees the far edge never lands. The same cosine works against you on brightness, because the light is spread over more area and illuminance falls by the cosine of the same angle. The practical consequence is that a fixture position chosen for convenience can cost both the shape and half a stop of the image, and the remedies -- optical keystone correction, a distorted gobo cut to compensate, or a better hanging position -- all cost more after the gobo is ordered than before. When the gobo's usable image is smaller than the fixture's gate, the projection scales by that fraction.

assumptions.name: Field angle
assumptions.value: the image fills the field, so diameter = 2 x throw x tan(field/2)

assumptions.name: Keystone
assumptions.value: the tilt-plane axis is throw x sin(phi) x [1/cos(incidence - phi) + 1/cos(incidence + phi)], more than the narrow-beam 1/cos(incidence); the perpendicular axis stays near its straight-on width

assumptions.name: Illuminance
assumptions.value: falls by cos(incidence) as the same light covers more area

sag-vertical-curve-comfort.formula: Comfort: L = A V^2 / 46.5 (A in %, V in mph, L in ft), K = L/A = V^2/46.5. Drainage maximum K <= 167 (a 0.30% minimum grade within 50 ft of the low point, 50/0.30 = 166.7), so the drainage-max length is 167 A.
sag-vertical-curve-comfort.edition: The AASHTO A Policy on Geometric Design of Highways and Streets (the Green Book) sag vertical-curve comfort and drainage controls, by name.
sag-vertical-curve-comfort.freeAccess: The AASHTO sag-curve comfort and drainage relations are published in the Green Book and mirrored in state DOT design manuals. The AHJ, state DOT design manual, and the licensed civil engineer of record govern.
sag-vertical-curve-comfort.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
sag-vertical-curve-comfort.editionNote: The AASHTO Green Book comfort criterion L = A V^2 / 46.5 (A the algebraic grade difference in percent, V the design speed in mph, L the curve length in ft), which limits the vertical (centripetal) acceleration on the sag to about 1 ft/s^2, with K = L/A = V^2/46.5. The drainage maximum K <= 167 corresponds to a 0.30% minimum grade reached within 50 ft of the low point (50/0.30 = 166.7), so the drainage-max length is 167 A; longer curves need drainage attention on curbed sections. These two criteria bracket the acceptable length. This tile does not apply the headlight stopping-sight-distance control, which is the governing sag criterion for stopping and typically the most restrictive (the separate sag-vertical-curve tile); the comfort length is only about half the headlight length in the normal range. A design aid, not a substitute for a licensed civil engineer's design.

assumptions.name: Comfort criterion
assumptions.value: L = A V^2 / 46.5 limits the vertical acceleration to about 1 ft/s^2; the 46.5 embeds that acceleration limit with V in mph and L in ft

assumptions.name: Drainage maximum
assumptions.value: K <= 167 from a 0.30% minimum grade within 50 ft of the low point (50/0.30 = 166.7); the drainage-max length is 167 A, applicable to curbed sections

assumptions.name: Not the SSD control
assumptions.value: the headlight stopping-sight-distance criterion (the governing sag stopping control) is a separate check, typically the most restrictive

pipe-flotation.formula: uplift_plf = water_unit_wt_pcf x (PI/4) x (od_in/12)^2; FS = (pipe_weight_plf + backfill_weight_plf) / uplift_plf; required_backfill_plf = target_fs x uplift_plf - pipe_weight_plf.
pipe-flotation.edition: Archimedes flotation identity by name (uplift = weight of displaced water; FS = resisting weight / uplift); first-principles buoyancy arithmetic.
pipe-flotation.freeAccess: Buoyancy is public first-principles physics; the design factor of safety comes from the project specification.
pipe-flotation.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
pipe-flotation.editionNote: Flotation is critical when the pipe is empty and the trench is flooded - a high water table or saturated backfill. Submerged backfill counts only its buoyant (effective) weight. The fixes are more cover, concrete anti-flotation collars, or ballasting the empty pipe until the backfill is complete. The design engineer governs.

assumptions.name: Uplift
assumptions.value: the full buoyant uplift of the empty pipe (water unit weight x displaced volume per foot)

assumptions.name: Resisting weight
assumptions.value: pipe self-weight plus backfill over the pipe; submerged backfill counts only its buoyant weight

assumptions.name: Target factor of safety
assumptions.value: 1.5 default; the project specification governs

tapered-roof-insulation.formula: avg_thk_in = start_thk_in + slope_in_per_ft x run_ft / 2; board_feet = area_sf x avg_thk_in; avg_r = avg_thk_in x r_per_in.
tapered-roof-insulation.edition: Tapered-insulation identity by name (average of a linear taper; board-feet and average R from the average thickness); first-principles arithmetic.
tapered-roof-insulation.freeAccess: The average-thickness arithmetic is public first-principles; the taper layout and R-per-inch come from the manufacturer's design.
tapered-roof-insulation.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
tapered-roof-insulation.editionNote: The taper layout (slope and start thickness) comes from the manufacturer's design to hit both the code drainage slope (a low-slope roof needs at least 1/4 in per foot) and the design R. Tapered polyiso is ordered by the board-foot (a square foot one inch thick). Distinct from the steady flat assembly-r-value.

assumptions.name: Taper layout
assumptions.value: slope (>= 1/4 in/ft for drainage) and start thickness from the manufacturer's design

assumptions.name: R per inch
assumptions.value: the insulation's R-value per inch (~5.7 for polyiso, aged)

press-fit-pressure.formula: p = (E x interference / D) x (Do^2 - D^2) / (2 Do^2); holding_force = p x pi x D x length x friction; hub_bore_stress = p x (Do^2 + D^2) / (Do^2 - D^2).
press-fit-pressure.edition: Lame interference-fit model (Machinery's Handbook 'Forces and Fits'; the Lame thick-cylinder equations, same-material solid shaft), by name; the actual materials, surface finish, and assembly method govern.
press-fit-pressure.freeAccess: The Lame thick-cylinder press-fit relations are published in standard machine-design references; the interference and modulus come from the fit and the material.
press-fit-pressure.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
press-fit-pressure.editionNote: Lame interference-fit model (same-material solid shaft). The diametral interference produces a contact pressure p = (E x interference / D) x (Do^2 - D^2) / (2 Do^2), an axial holding force = p x pi x D x length x friction, and a tangential (hoop) stress at the hub bore = p x (Do^2 + D^2) / (Do^2 - D^2). A thin hub (Do close to D) develops far less pressure for the same interference, so the holding force falls as the hub thins. The interference also raises a tangential stress at the hub bore that must stay below yield or the hub cracks. The model assumes elastic same-material parts and a solid shaft; a hollow shaft or dissimilar metals change the coefficients. A design aid, not the engineer of record; the actual materials, surface finish, and assembly method govern.

assumptions.name: Thin hub
assumptions.value: a hub OD close to the shaft develops far less contact pressure for the same interference

assumptions.name: Hub stress
assumptions.value: the interference raises a hoop stress at the hub bore that must stay below yield

assumptions.name: Same material solid shaft
assumptions.value: assumes elastic same-material parts and a solid shaft; hollow or dissimilar changes the coefficients

bearing-regrease.formula: grease_grams = 0.005 x od_mm x width_mm; base_interval_hr = K x (14,000,000 / (rpm x sqrt(bore_mm)) - 4 x bore_mm) with the bearing-type factor K = 10 radial ball, 5 cylindrical / needle roller, 1 spherical / tapered roller (SKF; STLE TLT April 2009 Fig. 7-8); corrected_interval_hr = base x correction_factor.
bearing-regrease.edition: Grease quantity from the bearing's free volume and the standard relubrication-interval relation for a horizontal, moderately loaded bearing at normal temperature, by name -- published bearing-maintenance practice, cited and not reproduced. The correction factor for temperature, orientation, load, and contamination is entered. The bearing manufacturer's own relubrication chart and a condition-monitoring program govern.
bearing-regrease.freeAccess: Both relations are published maintenance practice applied to the bearing's own dimensions and speed; no manufacturer's interval chart is reproduced.
bearing-regrease.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
bearing-regrease.editionNote: Two numbers, and both are commonly wrong in the field in opposite directions. The quantity is proportional to the bearing's outside diameter times its width, which is essentially its free internal volume, and it comes out much smaller than people expect -- grams rather than cartridges. Over-greasing is not the conservative choice it feels like: excess grease is churned by the rolling elements, it heats, and it either bleeds out or cooks into a varnish that starves the bearing, so a great many so-called lubrication failures are over-lubrication. The interval falls with both speed and bore, and the base relation describes a horizontal, moderately loaded bearing at normal temperature. The correction factor cuts it hard from there, and the corrections multiply: roughly halve for every fifteen degrees Celsius above about seventy, halve again for a vertical shaft, and cut substantially for heavy load, contamination, or vibration. Two identical bearings in different service can therefore have intervals a factor of ten apart, which is why a schedule built on the uncorrected number is not merely imprecise but wrong by a large multiple.

assumptions.name: Quantity
assumptions.value: 0.005 x OD x width in grams from millimetres -- the free volume, and much less than people expect

assumptions.name: Base interval conditions
assumptions.value: horizontal shaft, moderate load, normal temperature; the correction factor only ever shortens it

assumptions.name: Over-greasing
assumptions.value: excess grease churns, heats, and either bleeds or varnishes; many lubrication failures are over-lubrication

attic-ventilation.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
attic-ventilation.editionNote: Single-edition (engineering-practice / first-principles take-off; refresh as practice and product data shift).

assumptions.name: Ratio
assumptions.value: 1/150, reducible to 1/300 with a balanced split + vapor retarder (advisory)

idle-fuel-cost.formula: annual_idle_hours = idle_hours_per_day x operating_days; annual_gallons = annual_idle_hours x idle_gph; annual_cost = annual_gallons x fuel_price; fleet_cost = annual_cost x trucks; equivalent_miles = annual_idle_hours x miles_per_engine_hour; cents per mile = fleet_cost / fleet_annual_miles x 100.
idle-fuel-cost.edition: Idle fuel burn at the engine's idle consumption rate (near 0.8 gal/hr for a heavy-duty diesel, entered rather than bundled) and the conventional engine-hour-to-road-mile wear equivalence used in fleet maintenance planning, by name. The trucks' own telematics idle data and fuel records govern.
idle-fuel-cost.freeAccess: Multiplication on the fleet's own operating figures; the idle rate and the wear equivalence are entered rather than bundled.
idle-fuel-cost.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
idle-fuel-cost.editionNote: A heavy-duty diesel at idle burns something near eight tenths of a gallon an hour, more with the climate control loaded and more again on an older engine. That is a small number per hour and a very large one per year, and its accounting behaviour is what makes it worth isolating: because idling produces no miles, it is entirely absent from a cost per mile model built from fuel divided by odometer. It does not appear as its own line; it silently inflates the per-mile fuel number instead, which is why fleets that have never computed it are surprised by the size of it. The engine-hour line is the second cost and the more underestimated one. Maintenance intervals are driven by engine hours as much as by miles, and an idling hour is conventionally counted as somewhere around seven road miles of wear, so a truck idling several hours a day accrues the maintenance equivalent of a substantial extra route every year and reaches its overhaul far earlier than the odometer suggests. Expressing the result as cents per fleet mile is what makes the comparison actionable, because that is the same unit an auxiliary power unit or a bunk heater amortizes in.

assumptions.name: Idle rate
assumptions.value: near 0.8 gal/hr for a heavy-duty diesel; higher with HVAC load or an older engine; entered, not bundled

assumptions.name: Wear equivalence
assumptions.value: an idle hour conventionally counted as roughly 7 road miles of engine wear

assumptions.name: Invisible per-mile
assumptions.value: idling produces no miles, so it never appears in a fuel-divided-by-odometer cost model

guard-post-load.formula: uniform load at a post = 50 plf x post spacing; governing load = max(200 lb concentrated, uniform at post), the two being non-concurrent; base moment = governing load x post height; post S = b d^2 / 6 on ACTUAL dimensions; required Fb = moment / S; connection couple force = moment / fastener lever arm; force multiplier = post height / lever arm.
guard-post-load.edition: IBC 1607.9.1 - handrails and guards designed for a 50 pound per linear foot uniform load and a 200 pound concentrated load, with the uniform load not assumed to act concurrently with the concentrated load. Intermediate rails, balusters, panel fillers, and guard infill carry a separate 50 pound concentrated load under 1607.9.1.1 and 1607.9.1.2, which this tile names but does not check. Everything after the load is statics.
guard-post-load.freeAccess: The load values are short prescriptive sentences quoted throughout free code commentary and state adoptions. No table is reproduced, and no allowable stress is shipped - it is an input.
guard-post-load.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
guard-post-load.editionNote: Two findings, both easy to miss. First, the 200 pound concentrated load is not automatically the governing case: the 50 plf uniform load delivers 50 x spacing to each post, so the crossover is at 4 ft and any post spacing beyond that is governed by the uniform case. At the common 6 ft spacing it is 300 lb, half again the number most people design to. Second and more important, the post is almost never what fails. A 300 lb push at 36 in is 10,800 in-lb, which a 3.5 x 3.5 in post carries at about 1,511 psi of bending - high for common framing lumber but the right order of magnitude. The base connection has to resolve that SAME moment into a couple across only a few inches of fastener spacing, so at a 4 in spacing each side sees 2,700 lb, nine times the load that was applied. The lever arm collapsed from 36 in to 4 in and multiplied the force by exactly that ratio. That is the whole reason residential deck guards fail at the rim joist rather than at the post, why lag screws into the end grain of a rim are not an acceptable detail, and why the tested details use through-bolts with washers plus blocking, or a proprietary tension hold-down. Notching a post to clear the rim removes section exactly where the moment peaks, so the notched dimensions are the ones to enter. Scope: one post, one direction, bending only. The code applies the load in ANY direction including outward, inward, and vertically, so the modeled case may not be the worst one. Not checked: shear and bearing in the post, withdrawal and shear capacity of the specific fasteners, tension capacity of the rim or blocking, the load path back into the framing and diaphragm, deflection, or fatigue. Wood allowable stresses need the NDS adjustment factors and are an input here. A screen; the tested guard detail, the adopted code, and the engineer of record govern.

assumptions.value: 50 plf uniform and 200 lb concentrated, NOT concurrent

assumptions.name: Crossover
assumptions.value: the uniform case governs past 200/50 = 4 ft of post spacing

assumptions.name: Base moment
assumptions.value: governing load x post height above the connection

assumptions.name: Connection couple
assumptions.value: moment / fastener lever arm; multiplier = height / lever arm

assumptions.name: Allowable stress
assumptions.value: an INPUT; species, grade, and NDS adjustment factors are not shipped

assumptions.name: Not checked
assumptions.value: fastener capacity, rim and blocking tension, load path, deflection, fatigue, other load directions

assumptions.name: Infill
assumptions.value: the separate 50 lb load on balusters and panel fillers is named but not checked

smoke-alarm-placement.formula: minimum alarms = sleeping rooms + separate sleeping areas + additional stories; required cooking clearance = 20 ft (ionization), 10 ft (ionization with a silencing switch), or 6 ft (photoelectric, or marked to reduce cooking nuisance alarms); bathroom separation = 3 ft horizontally from the door or opening of a bathroom with a tub or shower.
smoke-alarm-placement.edition: IRC R314.3 Location and R314.3.1 Installation near cooking appliances.
smoke-alarm-placement.freeAccess: Both provisions are short prescriptive sentences reproduced in state adoptions and building-department bulletins. No table is reproduced.
smoke-alarm-placement.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
smoke-alarm-placement.editionNote: Two halves, and they get confused with each other. The COUNT under R314.3 is additive and is routinely undercounted: one alarm in each sleeping room, one OUTSIDE each separate sleeping area in the immediate vicinity of the bedrooms, and one on each additional story including basements and habitable attics but not crawl spaces or uninhabitable attics. Three bedrooms with one sleeping area and one extra story is five alarms as a floor, before interconnection or power requirements enter. The CLEARANCE under R314.3.1 is the half worth understanding, because it depends entirely on the SENSING TYPE and the spread is better than three to one - 20 ft horizontally from a permanently installed cooking appliance for an ionization alarm, 10 ft for an ionization alarm with an alarm-silencing switch, and 6 ft for a photoelectric alarm or one marked as helping to reduce cooking nuisance alarms. The practical consequence is the tile's most useful output: an alarm 8 ft from a range fails as ionization and passes as photoelectric, so in an open plan changing the sensing type is often the only way a location the code REQUIRES can also satisfy the nuisance separation - and it is far cheaper than relocating a required alarm. The tile says explicitly when a type change would fix a failure and when even 6 ft is not met, in which case the alarm simply has to move. Both separations carry the same exception: they do not apply where observing them would prevent placement in a location R314.3 requires. A required location wins over a nuisance separation, but that is a documented last resort rather than a default, and a type change usually removes the conflict first. Not checked: carbon monoxide alarms, which are a separate section with their own locations; interconnection so all alarms sound together; primary power from the building wiring with battery backup and the conditions permitting battery-only alarms in existing construction; the alteration, repair, and addition triggers for existing dwellings; ceiling and wall mounting geometry including sloped, peaked, and tray ceilings; state sealed-battery requirements; and heat detection where it substitutes. A screen; the adopted code, the alarm's listing, and the AHJ govern.

assumptions.name: Story exclusions
assumptions.value: crawl spaces and uninhabitable attics do not count

assumptions.name: Cooking clearance
assumptions.value: 20 ft ionization, 10 ft ionization with silencing, 6 ft photoelectric or nuisance-listed

assumptions.name: Bathroom
assumptions.value: 3 ft horizontally from the door or opening of a bathroom with a tub or shower

assumptions.name: Exception
assumptions.value: separations yield where they would prevent a required location - a documented last resort

assumptions.name: Not checked
assumptions.value: CO alarms, interconnection, power and battery backup, mounting geometry, existing-dwelling triggers

spanline-sag-for-tension.formula: d_min = (w L^2/8 + P L/4) / sqrt(T_allow^2 - (w L/2 + P/2)^2), the inverse of spanline-sag-tension with an optional midspan point load P; with P = 0 it is w L^2 / (8 sqrt(T_allow^2 - (w L/2)^2)).
spanline-sag-for-tension.edition: Shallow-cable parabola statics (by name) with ASME B30.9 / Wire Rope Users Manual rigging practice; first-principles, no edition cycle.
spanline-sag-for-tension.freeAccess: The shallow-cable parabola (H = w L^2 / 8d) is a public statics result; ASME B30.9 governs sling and rigging practice. An ESTIMATE only; the certified rope WLL and the head rigger govern.
spanline-sag-for-tension.governance: Estimate. Head rigger and manufacturer working-load-limit charts govern. Inspect every piece of hardware before the show.
spanline-sag-for-tension.editionNote: The least sag a spanline can be pulled to before the support (anchor) tension reaches the allowable, the inverse of spanline-sag-tension. Squaring T = w L^2 / (8 d) sqrt(1 + (4 d / L)^2) gives d_min = w L^2 / (8 sqrt(T_allow^2 - (w L / 2)^2)). The allowable limits the SUPPORT tension - the true maximum in the cable, at the anchors - not the horizontal component, and it must exceed the support vertical reaction w L / 2 (each anchor carries at least that much) or no sag can carry the load. Tension is inversely proportional to the sag, so any tighter than d_min overloads the rope and anchors. Enter the allowable as the certified rope WLL or the anchor capacity, whichever is lower, with the design factor already applied. Valid where the resulting sag is under about a tenth of the span (a deep sag trends toward the catenary); uniform load, level supports. A planning screen; the wire-rope working load limit, the anchor capacity, and the head rigger govern.

assumptions.name: Support-tension limit
assumptions.value: the allowable limits the support (anchor) tension and must exceed the w L / 2 vertical reaction; below that no sag can carry the load

assumptions.name: Shallow parabola
assumptions.value: valid where the resulting sag is under about a tenth of the span; a deep sag trends toward the catenary

assumptions.name: Uniform load, level supports
assumptions.value: the load is uniform along the horizontal span and the two supports are at the same height

assumptions.name: Estimate only
assumptions.value: the certified rope WLL, the anchor capacity, and the head rigger govern the actual pick

beam-clamp-side-pull.formula: V = T x sin(angle); H = T x cos(angle); pull_from_vertical = atan2(H, V); vertical_util = V / vertical_WLL x 100; horizontal_util = side_pull_rating > 0 ? H / side_pull_rating x 100 : flagged (no rating).
beam-clamp-side-pull.edition: Static force resolution; ASME B30.20 / beam-clamp manufacturer practice (the WLL is a vertical rating; side pull prohibited unless the manufacturer rates it), by name.
beam-clamp-side-pull.freeAccess: Force resolution is a public statics result; ASME B30.20 and the manufacturer's documentation govern below-the-hook hardware. An ESTIMATE only; the hardware ratings and a qualified rigger govern.
beam-clamp-side-pull.governance: Estimate. Head rigger and manufacturer working-load-limit charts govern. Inspect every piece of hardware before the show.

The leg tension and angle come from bridle-leg-tension or three-point-bridle. A design aid, not a rigging sign-off.

assumptions.value: the clamp WLL applies to a straight-down pull; any documented side-pull allowance is the manufacturer's, not a default

wallpaper-rolls.freeAccess: The strip method and the one-repeat-per-strip waste rule are public wallcovering-estimating practice. The roll dimensions are the product's stated bolt size.
wallpaper-rolls.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
wallpaper-rolls.editionNote: Single-edition (the strips-and-rolls relations do not roll). The roll dimensions are the product's stated bolt size (single/double/Euro rolls vary), door and window openings are a manual strip credit, and this is a material takeoff, not a hang plan.

assumptions.value: strips = ceil(perimeter / roll width); full-height strips across the run

assumptions.value: strip length = wall height + one pattern repeat; one repeat is wasted per strip to match the run

wood-row-group-tearout.formula: Z'NT = Ft' t (d - nrow Dh); Z'RTi = ni Fv' t scrit, scrit = min(end distance, in-row spacing) (end distance alone for a one-bolt row); Z'RT = sum of Z'RTi; Z'GT = Z'RT-1/2 + Z'RT-n/2 + Ft' t (nrow - 1)(srow - Dh); the connection takes the least of these and the bolt group capacity n Z' when entered.
wood-row-group-tearout.edition: ANSI/AWC NDS (2018) Appendix E, local stresses in fastener groups (Eq. E.2-1, E.3-2, E.3-3, E.4-1), by name, as worked in AWC Wood Design Focus, Winter 2002, "Is Your Wood Connection All Stressed Out? It Needn't Be: Appendix E Provisions".
wood-row-group-tearout.freeAccess: The NDS is free to view at awc.org; the Wood Design Focus article with its worked examples is a free PDF at awc.org.
wood-row-group-tearout.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
wood-row-group-tearout.editionNote: Checked against Wood Design Focus Example 1: a 3-1/8 x 12 in Combination 3 Douglas fir glulam, Fv' 240 psi, Ft' 1,450 psi, eight 1 in bolts in 1-1/16 in holes in three staggered rows (3, 2, 3) at 2.5 in row spacing, 7 in end distance and 4 in spacing, n Z' 35,040 lb: Z'NT 39,930 lb, Z'RT 24,000 lb, Z'GT 22,030 lb, group tear-out governs; this computes 39,932, 24,000 and 22,027 lb. Also reproduces the 2015 NDS splice in STRUCTURE magazine (Design of Bolted Connections per the 2015 NDS): 2x12 No. 2 Southern Pine, two rows of three 1 in bolts, Fv' 218.75 psi, Ft' 562.5 psi, s_critical 4 in: Z'RT 7,875 lb and Z'GT 6,416 lb against the printed 6,418 (the article rounds A_group-net to 4.41 sq in).

assumptions.name: Shear lines
assumptions.value: two per row at an apparent stress of Fv'/2 over the shortest clear length

assumptions.name: Net section
assumptions.value: one hole deducted per row, conservative for a staggered pattern

assumptions.name: Design values
assumptions.value: Fv' and Ft' entered already adjusted (CD, CM, Ct, and member-specific reductions)

dp-flow-meter.formula: Q = Cd A2 sqrt( 2 dP / (rho (1 - beta^4)) ); A2 = pi/4 d^2 (throat area); beta = d/D (bore/pipe-ID ratio); the 1 - beta^4 term is the velocity-of-approach factor. Incompressible liquid.
dp-flow-meter.edition: The differential-pressure primary-element (orifice / venturi / flow-nozzle) flow equation; ISO 5167 defines the precise discharge coefficient Cd and installation, but the Bernoulli equation itself is public physics, cited by name.
dp-flow-meter.freeAccess: The Bernoulli DP-flow equation is first-principles fluid mechanics; a typical Cd (0.61 orifice, 0.98 venturi, 0.97 nozzle) is editable and the meter's own calibration governs the exact value.
dp-flow-meter.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
dp-flow-meter.editionNote: Volumetric flow of an incompressible liquid through a restriction from the differential pressure across it: Q = Cd A2 sqrt(2 dP / (rho (1 - beta^4))). The restriction accelerates the fluid and drops its pressure; the drop backs out the flow, so flow tracks the SQUARE ROOT of dP (four times the flow reads as sixteen times the dP). beta = bore/pipe-ID sets the range and the permanent pressure loss, and the 1 - beta^4 term corrects for the approach velocity the fluid already has. The discharge coefficient Cd captures the vena contracta and friction: about 0.61 for a square-edge orifice, 0.98 for a classical venturi, 0.97 for a flow nozzle, so a venturi passes far more flow at the same dP and recovers most of the pressure. This is the incompressible-liquid form; a compressible gas needs a separate expansion factor Y, and a precise Cd (a function of beta and Reynolds number) comes from ISO 5167 or the meter's calibration. A field / sizing estimate; the calibrated meter governs.

assumptions.name: DP-flow equation
assumptions.value: Q = Cd A2 sqrt(2 dP/(rho (1 - beta^4))); flow ~ sqrt(dP)

assumptions.name: Discharge coefficient
assumptions.value: Cd ~ 0.61 orifice, 0.98 venturi, 0.97 nozzle (editable); or, for a square-edge orifice (added 2026-10-09), computed by the ISO 5167-2 Reader-Harris/Gallagher equation for flange, corner, or D and D/2 taps, iterated with Re = 4Q/(pi D nu); calibration governs

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: incompressible liquid only; a gas needs an expansion factor Y

seismic-overturning-stability.formula: effective dead-load coefficient = 0.9 - 0.2 SDS (LRFD combination 7) or 0.6 - 0.7 x 0.2 SDS (the ASD 0.6D + 0.7E pair); W_eff = coefficient x D; resisting moment = W_eff x lever arm (half the footprint unless entered); design overturning = M0 x 0.7 for ASD x 0.75 when the ASCE 7 12.13.4 soil-interface reduction is taken; ratio = resisting / demand; eccentricity = demand / W_eff, compared to the B/6 kern and to B/2.
seismic-overturning-stability.edition: ASCE 7 - the 0.9D + 1.0E uplift combination and the ASD 0.6D + 0.7E pair, with the vertical seismic effect Ev = 0.2 SDS D acting upward in the overturning case, and the reduction in overturning permitted at the soil-structure interface by Section 12.13.4: 25% for an equivalent lateral force design that is not an inverted pendulum or cantilevered column system, 10% for a modal design, none by default.
seismic-overturning-stability.freeAccess: The load-combination structure and the Ev = 0.2 SDS D definition are widely reproduced in free code commentary and university course material. The ASD effective coefficient is COMPOSED here from two separately stated pieces (the 0.6D combination and the 0.7 factor ASD applies to seismic) and the arithmetic is shown in the tile's note rather than presented as a memorized constant, so a user can audit it against their own edition.
seismic-overturning-stability.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
seismic-overturning-stability.editionNote: The point of the tile is the dead load that actually resists. It is not D. The vertical component of the same shaking lifts the building, so ASCE 7 pairs the uplift combination with Ev acting upward and the usable gravity drops to (0.9 - 0.2 SDS) D under LRFD - at SDS = 1.0 that is 0.70 D, a 22% cut against the 0.9 alone. Leaving Ev out is the classic way an overturning check passes on paper and should not, and the tile prints the subtraction so it is visible. The second point is that a passing ratio can still hide a problem: the worked example clears global stability at 1.55, yet the resultant sits 6.45 ft off the center of a 20 ft base against a B/6 kern of 3.33 ft, so part of the footing is already in uplift and the toe pressure is higher than any uniform check would show. A ratio alone does not reveal that, which is why the eccentricity is reported beside it. The 12.13.4 reduction is optional here and applies at the SOIL-STRUCTURE INTERFACE ONLY - carrying it up into the shear wall, its chords, or its hold-downs is a real and common error. Scope: global stability and resultant location only. Sliding, the soil bearing capacity under the concentrated toe pressure, the hold-down forces themselves, and pile or tiedown capacity are separate checks with their own tiles. The lever arm defaults to half the footprint, which assumes a centered resultant dead load; an eccentric building needs its arm entered. A design aid, not a substitute for a licensed engineer's design; the engineer of record governs.

assumptions.value: (0.9 - 0.2 SDS) D from combination 7 with Ev upward

assumptions.name: ASD effective dead load
assumptions.value: (0.6 - 0.7 x 0.2 SDS) D, composed from the 0.6D combination and the 0.7 seismic factor
assumptions.source: composed; arithmetic shown in the note

assumptions.name: Soil-interface reduction
assumptions.value: optional: 25% (ELF, not an inverted pendulum or cantilevered column) or 10% (modal), at the interface only; off by default

assumptions.name: Lever arm
assumptions.value: half the footprint by default; assumes a centered resultant dead load

assumptions.name: Kern check
assumptions.value: eccentricity against B/6 for full bearing and B/2 for a resultant off the base

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: global stability and resultant location; sliding, toe pressure, and hold-downs are separate

wood-beam-bending.formula: RB = sqrt(le x d / b^2); FbE = 1.20 x Emin' / RB^2; r = FbE/Fb*; CL = (1 + r)/1.9 - sqrt(((1 + r)/1.9)^2 - r/0.95) (clamped to 1.0); Fb' = Fb* x CL; S = b d^2 / 6; M' = Fb' x S.
wood-beam-bending.edition: NDS 3.3.3 beam stability factor CL and the slenderness / critical-buckling relations, by name; the reference bending value and its adjustment factors come from the NDS Supplement.
wood-beam-bending.freeAccess: The CL, RB, and FbE equations are stated in NDS 3.3.3, published free read-only by AWC at awc.org; the section-modulus and moment arithmetic is public statics.
wood-beam-bending.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
wood-beam-bending.editionNote: The NDS beam stability factor CL with RB = sqrt(le d / b^2) (capped at 50), FbE = 1.20 Emin' / RB^2, and CL = (1 + FbE/Fb*)/1.9 - sqrt(((1 + FbE/Fb*)/1.9)^2 - (FbE/Fb*)/0.95) (NDS 3.3.3), and the effective-length le from the loading / bracing conditions of NDS Table 3.3.3. Emin' default 620,000 psi (a common visually-graded Douglas Fir-Larch reference minimum modulus). Fb* is the reference bending value already multiplied by every applicable adjustment factor except CL - the user supplies it, and the reference values and the factors CD, CM, Ct, CF, Cfu, Ci, Cr come from the NDS Supplement for the actual species, grade, and service condition; le is the effective unbraced length from NDS Table 3.3.3 (not the clear span) for the actual bracing and loading. This checks lateral-torsional buckling of a solid rectangular sawn-lumber bending member bent about its strong axis only, and does not cover the volume factor CV or curvature / interaction of glulam, biaxial bending, or combined bending-plus-axial. A design aid, not a substitute for the engineer of record.

assumptions.name: Beam slenderness
assumptions.value: RB = sqrt(le d / b^2), capped at 50; geometry more slender than that is not a bending member

assumptions.name: Fb* user-supplied
assumptions.value: Fb* is the reference bending value times every applicable factor except CL; the reference and CD/CM/Ct/CF/Cfu/Ci/Cr come from the NDS Supplement

assumptions.name: Effective length
assumptions.value: le is the effective unbraced length of the compression edge from NDS Table 3.3.3, not the clear span

assumptions.value: medical-gas piping is brazed and certified by ASSE 6010-qualified plumbers/pipefitters; a verifier and the AHJ govern

kiln-charge-water.formula: oven-dry weight = green weight / (1 + moisture content / 100); water to remove = oven-dry weight x the moisture-content points removed / 100, at 8.3454 lb per US gallon; energy = that mass x an entered BTU per pound of water; vent load = the water divided by the schedule hours.
kiln-charge-water.edition: The oven-dry-basis moisture relation by name, with the Forest Products Laboratory dry-kiln schedules named as what governs the drying itself. The applicable drying schedule, the kiln manufacturer, and the mill's own kiln samples govern.
kiln-charge-water.freeAccess: Mass and energy arithmetic on the charge weight and moisture contents the user enters; no published schedule or manufacturer table is reproduced.
kiln-charge-water.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
kiln-charge-water.editionNote: The oven-dry basis is the trap. Wood moisture content is water weight divided by OVEN-DRY wood weight, not by total weight, so 100% moisture content means the water weighs as much as the wood, and green hardwood above 100% is entirely ordinary. Computing the water from green weight times the moisture percentage overstates it by exactly the initial moisture content, because green weight is oven-dry weight times one plus that fraction; both figures are reported so the size of that error is visible rather than argued. Once the water tonnage is known everything else follows. The energy is that mass times a heat requirement well above the latent heat of water, because a conventional kiln also heats the wood, heats the kiln, and loses heat out the vents along with the moisture; the vent load is what sizes the venting and, in a dehumidification kiln, the compressor. The third use is schedule sanity: most of the water leaves before fibre saturation and most of the TIME is spent after it, so a charge with twice the water takes far more than twice as long at the same nominal rate. A dehumidification kiln's energy is electrical and follows entirely different arithmetic.

assumptions.name: Moisture content is oven-dry basis
assumptions.value: so it can exceed 100%, and green weight times the percentage is wrong

assumptions.name: Energy is well above latent heat
assumptions.value: roughly 1,500 to 2,500 BTU per pound of water for a conventional kiln

assumptions.name: The measurement is kiln samples
assumptions.value: moisture content is measured with samples and a meter, not calculated

pool-cover-evaporation.formula: evaporative loss = surface area x evaporation depth x 7.481 gal/ft^3 x 8.34 lb/gal x 1,046 BTU/lb of latent heat; a cover's saving is that loss times its effectiveness times the fraction of the day it is on, and the FUEL saving divides by the heater efficiency.
pool-cover-evaporation.edition: Pool evaporative heat loss on the latent heat of vaporisation. The evaporation RATE is ENTERED because it depends on wind speed, humidity and the water-to-air temperature difference together, and is by far the largest uncertainty in the result.
pool-cover-evaporation.freeAccess: One latent heat constant and two unit conversions.
pool-cover-evaporation.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
pool-cover-evaporation.editionNote: Evaporation is the largest heat loss on most outdoor pools and it is the one nobody sees -- radiation, convection and conduction to the ground are all real and all smaller, while an owner reasoning about pool heat loss reasons about the air temperature. That is why the most effective single measure is a cover and the second is a windbreak. A COVER ONLY WORKS WHILE IT IS ON: effectiveness and hours MULTIPLY, so a 90% cover on for two thirds of the day saves 60% of the loss, not 90%. The hours that matter most are overnight, when the air is coldest and driest. And the FUEL saving is larger than the heat saving by the heater's efficiency -- heat not lost is fuel not bought. The gallons are a second saving the heat figure hides: they are treated, balanced water, replaced with cold make-up that must then be heated and re-balanced.

assumptions.name: Evaporation rate is entered
assumptions.value: it depends on wind, humidity and the temperature difference; pool-evaporation-rate estimates it from those conditions
assumptions.source: a site measurement, ASHRAE Applications, or pool-evaporation-rate

assumptions.name: Cover effectiveness times hours
assumptions.value: a cover off the pool saves nothing

assumptions.name: Make-up water is not all evaporation
assumptions.value: splash-out, backwash and leaks read the same

arc-rated-clothing-selection.formula: the system arc rating must be at or above the incident energy at the working distance; margin = system rating - incident energy, and the minimum required rating IS the incident energy.
arc-rated-clothing-selection.edition: Arc-rated clothing selection under NFPA 70E. Incident energy is ENTERED because computing it is a separate study. ATPV is the incident energy at a 50% probability of a second-degree burn; where a fabric reports both ATPV and EBT, the LOWER is its arc rating.
arc-rated-clothing-selection.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
arc-rated-clothing-selection.editionNote: What the rating means is the part that changes decisions: ATPV is not a threshold below which nothing happens, it is a fifty percent burn probability, so clothing rated exactly at the exposure places the wearer on that point. Margin is not conservatism, it is the difference between a coin toss and a protected worker. LAYERING IS NOT ADDITION -- two 8 cal garments do not make a 16 cal system, because the rating of a combination comes from testing it and the air gaps between layers contribute in a way no arithmetic predicts. Substituting an underlayer changes the system that was tested. THE UNDERLAYER PROHIBITION IS ABSOLUTE and routinely missed: polyester, nylon and acetate next to skin melt and adhere in an arc event, and the items forgotten are the undershirt and the socks. And arc rating addresses the THERMAL hazard only -- the pressure wave, noise, molten metal spray and shock hazard are separate.

assumptions.name: Incident energy is entered
assumptions.value: computing it is a separate study
assumptions.source: an IEEE 1584 study or the table method

assumptions.name: System ratings are tested, not summed
assumptions.value: air gaps between layers contribute unpredictably
assumptions.source: the garment manufacturer's tested system rating

assumptions.name: Thermal hazard only
assumptions.value: pressure, noise, spray and shock are separate
assumptions.source: NFPA 70E and the electrical safety programme

optical-return-loss.formula: bare-end Fresnel R = ((n - 1)/(n + 1))^2; event reflectances convert by 10^(dB/10), add in linear power, and link ORL = -10 log10(sum R).
optical-return-loss.edition: Fresnel reflection and linear addition of reflected optical powers.
optical-return-loss.freeAccess: A Fresnel ratio and power/dB conversions.
optical-return-loss.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
optical-return-loss.editionNote: ONE OPEN END DOMINATES THE LINK. Four -50 dB connectors combine to 44.0 dB ORL, but a flat glass-air end at n = 1.468 reflects 3.60% and drops the link to 14.4 dB. The 4 good connectors then contribute only about 0.11% of reflected power. Decibels are not added directly.

assumptions.name: Nominal event reflectance
assumptions.value: cleanliness, endface geometry and mating condition alter it

assumptions.name: No round-trip attenuation
assumptions.value: distant reflections are conservatively not reduced

assumptions.name: Equipment response excluded
assumptions.value: laser sensitivity to reflection is product-specific

cable-jetting-distance.formula: fill = cable OD / duct ID (the manufacturers' basis); area fill = (OD/ID)^2 shown beside it; annulus = pi(ID^2 - OD^2)/4; nominal duct flow = annulus x velocity; free-air delivery scales by absolute pressure ratio.
cable-jetting-distance.edition: Microduct fill and nominal air-demand screen. Jetting distance is deliberately not calculated.
cable-jetting-distance.freeAccess: Circle areas and a volumetric-flow conversion.
cable-jetting-distance.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
cable-jetting-distance.editionNote: THE ANNULUS IS THE MACHINE. Fill is OD over ID, as Corning AEN096 (target 50 to 80%) and Dura-Line (50 to 75%) state it; the spec's area ratio against a 40 to 60% window matched no publisher and flagged Corning's own recommended pairs. The worked 8.5 mm cable fills a 10 mm duct to 85%, above Corning's 80%; a 65% target is a 6.5 mm cable at about 680 L/min free air. Real compressor demand is manufacturer data.

assumptions.name: Nominal incompressible screen
assumptions.value: real duct flow is compressible and pressure falls along the run

assumptions.name: Fill window is entered
assumptions.value: cable and duct surface and stiffness alter it

assumptions.name: Distance excluded
assumptions.value: bends, elevation and surface friction prevent a general formula
assumptions.source: manufacturer charts and a trial shot

mash-tun-grain-bed.formula: mash gal per lb = R/4 + displacement; depth = G x gal per lb / 7.48 / (pi D^2 / 4); max grain = area x depth limit x 7.48 / gal per lb.
mash-tun-grain-bed.edition: Geometry, with grain displacement about 0.08 gal per lb and 12 to 18 in the usual working bed depth. The lauter tun manufacturer's rated depth governs.
mash-tun-grain-bed.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
mash-tun-grain-bed.editionNote: The depth limit caps the strongest single-mash beer, and area goes as the square of diameter, so a modestly wider tun takes a much larger grain bill.

assumptions.name: Vessel
assumptions.value: a flat-bottomed cylinder

landfill-gas-generation.formula: Q = sum over placement years of k x L0 x M x e^(-k t); capacity = methane flow x heating value x generator efficiency, decayed forward as e^(-k t).
landfill-gas-generation.edition: First-order decay, with the AP-42 inventory defaults of a methane yield of 100 cubic metres per megagram and a methane generation rate constant of 0.04 (roughly 0.02 arid, 0.05 to 0.07 wet or bioreactor). The Clean Air Act regulatory defaults for the NMOC calculation, 40 CFR 60.764, are higher: 170 cubic metres per megagram and 0.05 (0.02 under 25 in of annual precipitation).
landfill-gas-generation.freeAccess: The model and its defaults are published by the EPA and are freely available.
landfill-gas-generation.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
landfill-gas-generation.editionNote: Generation and collection are different quantities and mixing them is the usual error in a project proposal; the uncollected share is also the site's methane emission and its regulatory exposure.

assumptions.name: Decay constant
assumptions.value: where the uncertainty lives; it depends overwhelmingly on moisture and a factor of two or three between an arid and a wet site is ordinary

assumptions.name: Peak
assumptions.value: modelled at closure, when every placement year contributes and none has decayed far

assumptions.name: Time step
assumptions.value: whole years, the newest counted at age zero; EPA's LandGEM steps in tenths of a year and reads 2.2% lower at closure at k = 0.04, 3.8% at 0.07, and 31% at its wet-inventory 0.7

pier-scour-depth.formula: y_s / y_1 = 2.0 K1 K2 K3 (a / y_1)^0.65 Fr_1^0.43, with Fr = V / sqrt(g y) and K2 = (cos theta + (L/a) sin theta)^0.65.
pier-scour-depth.edition: FHWA HEC-18 Evaluating Scour at Bridges, with K1 the nose shape (1.0 round, 1.1 square, 0.9 sharp) and K3 the bed condition (1.1 plane bed and antidunes).
pier-scour-depth.freeAccess: HEC-18 is published by the Federal Highway Administration and is freely available.
pier-scour-depth.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
pier-scour-depth.editionNote: This is the LOCAL component only. Contraction scour across the bridge opening and long-term degradation of the reach are separate components and they ADD; a foundation designed against local scour alone is designed against a fraction of the depth the bed will reach.

assumptions.name: Angle of attack
assumptions.value: a geometry problem rather than a hydraulic one, and channels migrate -- a pier aligned when built is not necessarily aligned now

assumptions.name: Scour mechanism
assumptions.value: removes the soil providing both the bearing and the lateral support, often during the flood when the bed cannot be seen

assumptions.name: Limits
assumptions.value: L/a enters K2 at no more than 12; K1 is 1.0 past 5 degrees of skew; a round-nosed pier aligned with the flow is held to 2.4 pier widths at Fr <= 0.8 and 3.0 above

responder-camp-sanitation.formula: toilets per sex = max(2, ceil(n_sex / 15)) for each sex housed; urinals = ceil(men / 25) or 2 ft of trough each; basins = ceil(total / 6); showerheads = ceil(total / 10); laundry trays = ceil(total / 30); fountains = ceil(total / 100) where water is under pressure; water = 35 gal x total per day at a peak of 2.5 x the average hourly rate; sleeping floor = 50 sq ft x total.
responder-camp-sanitation.edition: 29 CFR 1910.142, Temporary labor camps, paragraphs (b)(2), (b)(3), (c)(2), (c)(4), (d)(3), (d)(5), (d)(6), and (f)(1), read at law.cornell.edu on 2026-09-30 and reproduced as federal regulation. OSHA, the state plan, and the local health department govern.
responder-camp-sanitation.freeAccess: The Code of Federal Regulations is public domain; the camp ratios are restated from the Cornell LII copy.
responder-camp-sanitation.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
responder-camp-sanitation.editionNote: A camp is a small town and the standard sizes it like one. Toilets are counted separately for each sex against the maximum number of that sex the camp is designed to house, with a minimum of two in any shared facility, so the minimum rather than the ratio sets the small side of a camp; urinals are in addition to the men's toilets. The water figure sizes the infrastructure: 35 gallons per person per day at 2.5 times the average hourly rate, because demand bunches at shift change, and that peak sizes a trailer's pump or a bladder's refill schedule. Fifty square feet of sleeping floor per occupant is routinely violated when a camp is filled past its design population in the first days of a response.

assumptions.name: Design population by sex
assumptions.value: the maximum of each sex the camp is designed to house at one time

assumptions.name: Peak water rate
assumptions.value: 2 1/2 times the average hourly demand of 35 gal per person per day

assumptions.name: Whether the standard applies
assumptions.value: a regulatory question for the camp; agency base-camp standards and state plans may be more stringent

roof-snow-ice-weight.formula: load = sum of layer depth (ft) x unit weight (psf per ft): dry snow 3, settled 12.5 (mid of 10-15), wet 21, ice 57, ASCE 7 density 0.13 pg + 14 <= 30, or an entered 3-21 value (override for a measured core); ratio = load / roof design snow load.
roof-snow-ice-weight.edition: FEMA P-957, Snow Load Safety Guide (2013), Section 2.2 unit weights and warning signs; the ASCE 7 snow density relation cited by section as an optional basis. The building's design documents and a structural engineer govern.
roof-snow-ice-weight.freeAccess: FEMA P-957 is a free federal publication; ASCE 7 is cited by section only.
roof-snow-ice-weight.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed structural engineer govern.
roof-snow-ice-weight.editionNote: A foot of snow can weigh 3 psf or 21, and the difference is water; ice is almost as heavy as water, so two inches of it weighs about as much as three feet of light, dry snow. A roof after a long storm is a stack of layers, entered separately. The comparison is with the roof's design snow load, never the ground snow value on a map, which FEMA P-957 warns against. The tile reports a ratio; its 75% approach band is a prompt to plan, not a FEMA threshold. Sagging, new cracks, creaking, or sticking doors mean leaving the building regardless of the numbers, and clearing is itself hazardous, including uneven removal that leaves an unbalanced load.

assumptions.name: Snow unit weight
assumptions.value: about 3 psf per ft light and dry to 21 psf per ft wet and heavy

assumptions.name: Ice unit weight
assumptions.value: about 57 psf per ft, a little under 5 psf per inch

assumptions.name: Settled snow
assumptions.value: 12.5 psf per ft, the middle of the commonly cited 10-15 range
